articles.body:
Se credi di aver bisogno di supporto, il Progetto Itaca offre una linea di ascolto telefonica per le persone che soffrono di disagio psichico e per i loro familiari.

Gli operatori possono essere contattati al numero verde nazionale per la Salute Mentale 800.274.274 (da fisso) o 02.29007166 (da cellulare) dal lunedì al venerdì dalle ore 9.00 alle 22.00. La mail è linea.ascolto@progettoitaca.org

Cristina (nome di fantasia) non ha avuto una vita facile. Nel tentativo di rimettere insieme i frammenti della propria esistenza, segnata da una diagnosi di schizofrenia, due trattamenti sanitari obbligatori (TSO) e il temporaneo allontanamento del figlio, affidato ai servizi sociali, ha deciso di scrivere un’autobiografia. Nel libro Cristina racconta le vessazioni subite fin dall’infanzia e una vita che, nella sua ricostruzione, è stata segnata dalla presenza costante di persone intenzionate a farle del male.

Cristina è convinta di essere stata manipolata, nel corso degli anni, da familiari e colleghi di lavoro. Tra quelle che lei stessa definisce «supposizioni deliranti», c’è l’idea che i servizi segreti controllino le persone considerate pericolose, tra cui anche lei, riportando ogni suo pensiero e movimento. Forse, aggiunge, anche anche dietro l’invalidità di suo figlio potrebbero esserci loro, sarebbe un modo per tenere occupati i genitori ritenuti scomodi. «Non so se davvero la mia vita possa essere riletta in questa chiave delirante, se le mie supposizioni si riveleranno tutte vere o se magari lo sono solo alcune», scrive nel suo libro, che ha condiviso con Facta. Nel frattempo, Cristina è rimasta senza lavoro, molte persone l’hanno allontanata, suo marito l’ha lasciata e oggi si sente profondamente stanca della vita.

Negli ultimi anni, sia all’estero che in Italia, si è sviluppata un’attiva comunità online di targeted individuals (“individui bersaglio”, in italiano), persone convinte di essere oggetto di uno stalking di gruppo, o come viene chiamato comunemente tra i suoi membri, gang stalk. I responsabili delle presunte persecuzioni vengono solitamente individuati nei servizi segreti, i vicini di casa o il servizio sanitario. Oltre a essere convinti di venire controllati o spiati, molti targeted individuals parlano dell’uso di “armi neurali” – spesso chiamate armi ELF a frequenza estremamente bassa (Extremely Low Frequency in inglese) – nei loro confronti, che li porterebbero a sentire delle voci dentro la propria testa, o li spingerebbero a compiere azioni contro la propria volontà.

Durante la Guerra fredda, a partire dagli anni ‘50, la CIA finanziò un programma segreto e illegale di ricerca e sperimentazione umana, noto come MK-ULTRA, il cui obiettivo era sviluppare tecniche e sostanze per il controllo mentale, la manipolazione psicologica e l’estrazione di informazioni durante gli interrogatori. Molte delle vittime, cittadini americani ignari di far parte di un test segreto, vennero esposte ad alti dosaggi di LSD, ipnosi, elettroshock e deprivazione sensoriale.

Uno degli scienziati impegnati nel progetto, Sidney Gottlieb, era interessato a scoprire quanta LSD potesse assumere un essere umano. Esisteva un punto di rottura, una dose talmente massiccia da mandare in frantumi la mente e spazzare via la coscienza, così da impiantare una nuova personalità? Negli anni ‘70 il programma venne interrotto e la maggior parte dei documenti venne distrutta, anche se un’inchiesta del New York Times del 1974 ne svelò l’esistenza. Tuttavia, per la comunità dei targeted individuals, questi esperimenti in realtà non sarebbero mai terminati, e la presunta persecuzione ai loro danni ne è una prova.

I targeted individuals citano spesso anche la cosiddetta sindrome dell’Avana, l’improvviso e inspiegabile malessere che colpì alcuni membri dell’ambasciata statunitense all’Avana nel 2016. Tra i sintomi, le vittime citarono vertigini, mal di testa, nausea e alterazioni sensoriali. Negli anni successivi, diversi agenti della CIA dislocati in varie parti del mondo hanno dichiarato di aver subito qualcosa di simile, con sintomi la cui durata va da settimane ad anni. Se anche all’interno dell’intelligence statunitense si è cercato di stabilire una relazione tra il malessere degli agenti e l’uso di armi sconosciute a energia sonora da parte della Russia o altre potenze, l’idea è stata scartata e definita fantascienza da vari esperti. Ciononostante, i targeted individuals sono sicuri che queste armi esistano, e vengano usate contro di loro.

Le community online delle presunte vittime di stalking di gruppo

La comunità online delle presunte vittime di stalking di gruppo è particolarmente sviluppata negli Stati Uniti. Esistono subreddit – forum online dedicati ad argomenti specifici all’interno della piattaforma Reddit – con decine di migliaia di membri e moltissimi account social che raccontano la propria quotidianità fatta di presunti pedinamenti e sorveglianza. Molti targeted individuals filmano quelli che ritengono i propri pedinatori e postano i filmati sui social per provare le persecuzioni, anche se in realtà i presunti sorveglianti sono chiaramente dei semplici passanti, oppure automobili che procedono nella stessa direzione. Gli individui bersaglio hanno anche fatto rete e da anni sono attive organizzazioni di tutela delle presunte vittime di gang stalk.

Anche in Italia si muove sottotraccia una comunità variegata; ci sono account TikTok che spiegano le tecniche con cui i servizi segreti entrerebbero nella loro casa, ma anche varie pagine Facebook e gruppi di supporto su WhatsApp. Giorgio (nome di fantasia) è uno dei fondatori di un progetto mandato avanti da, si legge sul sito, «vittime di armi psicotroniche/elettromagnetiche, ultrasoniche e infrasoniche». Ha spiegato a Facta che la comunità online italiana è attiva da circa una ventina di anni, «i primi a parlarne sono stati un gruppo contro le attività psicologiche segrete e un progetto di tutela delle vittime di armi elettroniche mentali». Giorgio conosce «un centinaio di vittime consapevoli di esserlo», ma secondo lui ci sarebbero «molte persone» che non sarebbero a conoscenza «della tecnologia psicotronica» e per questo «credono di essere malati psichiatrici».

La community sembra essere abbastanza grande da avere le sue antipatie o divergenze: Facta ha visionato un video in italiano su un canale YouTube dedicato alle presunte tecniche di controllo mentale in cui si accusa un membro della comunità online di millantare un microchip impiantato in testa, quando «in realtà sarebbe soltanto vittima di campi elettromagnetici dovuti alle frequenze a onde convogliate sparate attraverso armi a energia diretta». Giorgio racconta a Facta che «la sua tortura» è iniziata nel 2009, anno in cui ha iniziato a sentire delle voci nella testa ventiquattr’ore su ventiquattro, voci che a suo dire diventano urla quando qualcuno ne aumenta il volume. Inoltre, afferma di subire scosse elettriche quando si trova nel suo letto, ed è convinto di essere vittima di stalking organizzato. Secondo il suo racconto, riconosce le persone che lo controllano da alcuni comportamenti: «mi fissano e mi si avvicinano troppo senza motivo, oppure fanno dei gesti con le mani o dicono qualcosa di sospetto o destabilizzante».

A chi gli chiede un consiglio Giorgio suggerisce di mantenere la calma, evitare di urlare o compiere gesti violenti per non rischiare un trattamento sanitario obbligatorio (TSO). «Dico di uscire di casa, di non isolarsi, di fare attività fisica e distrarsi con musica rilassante, e poi di unirsi alla comunità italiana dei targeted individuals. Ma se la tortura psicotronica delle voci nella testa è tremenda, consiglio anche di continuare a prendere gli psicofarmaci perché almeno intontiscono e alleviano la tortura». Cristina ha spiegato a Facta che questi gruppi online all’inizio le avrebbero aperto gli occhi: «avevo finalmente la sensazione che qualcuno capisse e conoscesse la mia situazione». Di recente, però, frequentare quegli spazi la fa sentire impotente: davanti alla portata di quello che subisce, sente che non trova modo di avere giustizia. Alcuni targeted individuals si sono mossi anche per vie legali: Giorgio afferma di aver fatto degli esposti, che sono stati prontamente archiviati. Negli Stati Uniti ci sono state, tra le varie azioni legali portate avanti dalle presunte vittime di stalking di gruppo, anche una collettiva contro l’FBI e il Procuratore Generale, anche se la corte ha definito le accuse “fantasiose”.

Targeted individuals, problemi di salute mentale e radicalizzazione online

Intervistata in un articolo del 2016 del New York Times, Lorraine Sheridan, psicologa forense e co-autrice di uno dei primi studi sull’argomento, ha sottolineato come la mancanza di ricerche renda questo fenomeno ancora più pericoloso. Se chi soffre di anoressia o ha istinti suicidi può trovare online informazioni mediche o percorsi di cura, chi è convinto di essere un individuo bersaglio e cerca informazioni su internet trova solo pagine e pagine che validano la sua convinzione come un fatto reale e assodato. «Finiscono in una camera dell’eco chiusa su se stessa», ha spiegato. Sul sito di un’organizzazione internazionale di targeted individuals con ramificazioni anche in Europa, si consiglia addirittura di tagliare i rapporti coi propri familiari se si sospetta che siano coinvolti nella cospirazione. Ma soprattutto, di non parlare dei propri sintomi coi medici. Nel suo studio, Sheridan ha esaminato 128 casi segnalati di gang stalking, giungendo alla conclusione che tutti i soggetti soffrissero probabilmente di manie di persecuzione. Stefano Iacone, autore e psicoterapeuta presso l’ASL di Napoli, conferma a Facta che nello sviluppo di una mentalità complottista come quella degli individui bersaglio la dimensione collettiva è fondamentale, «senza sarebbero un fenomeno psichiatrico e basta».

Sempre negli Stati Uniti, si sono anche già verificati atti violenti da parte di individui bersaglio. L’ISD (Institute for Strategic Dialogue), un’organizzazione che si occupa di ricerca e analisi su radicalizzazione ed estremismo, ne ha documentati cinque compiuti da presunti o autoproclamati targeted individuals tra il 2013 e il 2024. Il caso più noto è quello di Aaron Alexis, un ex marinaio che nel 2013 uccise 12 persone al Washington Navy Yard, lasciando un documento in cui accusava la Marina di attaccarlo con onde elettromagnetiche. Sull’arma Alexis aveva inciso le frasi “la mia ELF” (ovvero la sua “arma neurale”) “e “fine del tormento”. È accertato che Alexis in passato avesse scritto delle mail al direttore di un’organizzazione di tutela dei targeted individuals. L’anno seguente, nel 2014, l’ex procuratore Myron May registrò un video per denunciare come il gang stalking gli avesse rovinato la vita, dopodiché entrò nella biblioteca della Florida State University, dove si era laureato nel 2005, e sparò a tre persone. Un ultimo caso, possibilmente collegato alla community, è avvenuto nel 2025, quando un uomo convinto di essere perseguitato dalle forze dell’ordine ha ucciso a colpi di pistola un agente della Polizia di Stato del Delaware.

Va chiarito che chi entra in questi spazi online è spesso esposto a molti altri complottismi o ideologie radicali, pertanto i fattori scatenanti delle violenze possono essere molteplici. Lo psicoterapeuta Stefano Iacone inoltre mette in guardia dai parallelismi: «gli Stati Uniti restano di gran lunga una società molto più violenta e atomizzata, il che favorisce atti di questo tipo». Allo stesso tempo, lo psicoterapeuta evidenzia come i dati epidemiologici nei Paesi occidentali mostrino un drammatico aumento dei disturbi mentali e, soprattutto, un abbassamento della loro età di esordio, a conferma di un progressivo deterioramento della salute mentale della popolazione.

*Facta ha deciso di non inserire link diretti ai siti o account social citati nell’articolo per tutelare le persone interessate.

articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
articles.preview: For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar. "Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500." It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang.
articles.body:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.

"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.

"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."

When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".

"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.

"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."

These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.

Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."

The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.

Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."

But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.

For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.

Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.

The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.

In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.

"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.

"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."

The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.

He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."

* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

articles.title: 'Geopolitics created the urgency': India's drone and robotics firms ride a wave of defence demand
articles.summary: Border tensions and government support are driving India's drone and robotics manufacturers towards defence applications. But experts warn that reliance on imported components and unpredictable military orders could hinder long-term growth.
articles.preview: Border tensions and government support are driving India's drone and robotics manufacturers towards defence applications. But experts warn that reliance on imported components and unpredictable military orders could hinder long-term growth. BENGALURU: Three four-legged robots raced around a specially designed track at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, drawing crowds as they competed to clock the fastest lap. Param, developed by Bengaluru-based General Autonomy, won the race.
articles.body:
Border tensions and government support are driving India's drone and robotics manufacturers towards defence applications. But experts warn that reliance on imported components and unpredictable military orders could hinder long-term growth.

BENGALURU: Three four-legged robots raced around a specially designed track at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, drawing crowds as they competed to clock the fastest lap.

Param, developed by Bengaluru-based General Autonomy, won the race. But for the company's co-founder Farid Ahsan, the real test lies far from the racetrack - on the military front line.

“What is more hazardous than the job of a soldier on the front lines?” he asked rhetorically.

General Autonomy, which began in industrial automation, is now working with the Indian armed forces to explore military applications for its robotic dogs and humanoids, including surveillance, patrolling and transporting supplies.

It was among several manufacturers showcasing unmanned technologies at the three-day summit from Nov 17 to 19, as India's drone and robotics firms look to tap growing demand from the country’s defence sector.

“The defence market is so big, with orders running into billions of rupees. The projected demand is also extremely high, and it's kind of engulfing the civil market,” Ezhilan Nanmaran, head of product and strategic alliances at Indian drone manufacturer IdeaForge, told CNA.

In August 2026, India's Ministry of Defence signed contracts worth approximately 15.8 billion Indian rupees (US$170 million) with Indian manufacturers Tata Advanced Systems and NIBE for armed drones and related equipment for the Indian Army.

IdeaForge itself secured a 1.37-billion-rupee contract from the ministry in June 2025 to supply the Indian Army with small surveillance drones and accessories, according to its stock-exchange filing.

But industry players told CNA that turning growing demand into a sustainable business will depend on developing reliable technology, reducing reliance on imported components and securing a steady flow of orders.

DEFENCE DEMAND DRIVES INDIA'S DRONE BOOM

The Indian government is pushing to boost domestic defence manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers.

“India must work in a mission mode to emerge as a global hub of indigenous drone manufacturing in the next few years,” Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said at an industry conclave in New Delhi on Mar 19.

To support innovation, the government has introduced funding schemes including Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) and Acing Development of Innovative Technologies with iDEX (ADITI), which offers eligible startups grants of up to 250 million rupees each.

The number of new Indian companies founded in the defence-drone sector more than tripled from eight in 2022 to 26 in 2025, with another 33 established in the first 11 months of 2026, according to data from market intelligence firm Tracxn.

Drone manufacturers are increasingly focusing on defence applications over civilian uses such as urban deliveries, where commercial adoption remains limited, analysts said.

Neil Shah, vice-president of research at Counterpoint Research, said India's low-cost motorcycle deliveries, restrictions on long-distance drone flights and lack of landing infrastructure hinder commercial adoption.

“Covering the last mile is very tough in India,” he said. He added that drones were better suited to transporting goods between fixed locations, particularly for time-sensitive deliveries such as medical samples.

By contrast, growing military requirements and government support has created a stronger market for defence manufacturers, according to Shweta Rajpal Kohli, president and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, an Indian startup advocacy group.

“Geopolitics created the urgency. Policy created the suppliers,” she told CNA, referring to changing security priorities and government initiatives that have helped startups develop technologies for the armed forces.

“We would like to get into it (civilian drone applications), but right now we have good traction with police forces and army, so that's where our focus is at,” said Arjun Naga Vinay, assistant sales manager at Bengaluru-based drone firm NeoSky.

The company develops surveillance and mapping drones and is owned by Indian conglomerate RattanIndia Enterprises.

Vinay told CNA that the company had supplied 60 surveillance drones to Karnataka Police and subsequently received a repeat order. It has also trained around 150 policewomen to operate drones.

NeoSky is also helping Indian Army units establish drone-training facilities, providing equipment, simulators and training in drone assembly, maintenance and operation.

Meanwhile, General Autonomy's Farid Ahsan said heightened regional security tensions along India’s border with Pakistan last year prompted the company to shift from industrial automation to defence.

“We understood that the biggest requirement for adopting robotics in India is at the front line,” he said, citing the harsh conditions and risks faced by soldiers.

The company is exploring military applications for its robots with the Indian armed forces, although the machines remain under development and have yet to enter operational service.

HOW DRONES ARE RESHAPING MODERN WARFARE

Drones have become increasingly important in modern warfare, with conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East demonstrating their ability to carry out surveillance, strike targets and challenge traditional military defences.

The Russia-Ukraine war has been a turning point. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, both sides have deployed large numbers of drones to track enemy movements, direct artillery fire and strike troops, tanks and critical military and civilian infrastructure.

Relatively inexpensive drones have also allowed Ukrainian forces to strike Russian targets without relying solely on costly missiles or conventional aircraft. According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, drones had overtaken artillery as the leading cause of front-line casualties by 2025, accounting for up to 80 per cent of losses.

In the Middle East, Israel has used drones for surveillance and strikes in Gaza, while Iran has deployed explosive-laden drones against Israel and other targets in the region.

Iranian-designed Shahed drones - also used extensively by Russia in Ukraine - have demonstrated how large numbers of relatively cheap unmanned aircraft can overwhelm air defences and force opponents to expend costly interceptor missiles.

These conflicts have prompted governments worldwide to step up investment in military drones.

In February, Germany approved an initial 540 million euro order for attack drones, according to a Reuters report. While the US has earmarked US$1 billion to acquire about 340,000 small military drones over two years.

The United Kingdom announced plans in June 2025 to invest more than 4 billion pounds in autonomous military systems, including drones. In June 2026, it also pledged to supply Ukraine with 150,000 drones as part of a broader 752 million pound military aid package, according to its Ministry of Defence.

The surge in spending is creating opportunities for defence manufacturers, although rapidly evolving battlefield threats mean they must continually develop systems capable of resisting electronic interference and other countermeasures.

INDIA'S DRONE MAKERS PREPARE FOR TOUGHER MISSIONS

As India's military needs evolve, drone manufacturers are developing more advanced systems capable of operating in increasingly hostile environments.

IdeaForge's Nanmaran said India's border conflicts with Pakistan and China had highlighted the need for drones capable of withstanding electronic jamming and GPS spoofing - techniques used to disrupt communications and manipulate navigation systems.

“Flying a drone on your own border, looking at your border, is very different from flying in a contested environment,” he said.

Drone companies are also exploring applications beyond surveillance.

IdeaForge is developing a drone called Yeti to transport heavy supplies to remote areas.

Meanwhile, General Autonomy is exploring how four-legged robots and humanoids could patrol military installations, inspect hazardous areas and carry supplies across difficult terrain.

Ahsan said the company was adapting its machines to India's challenging geographical terrain, including mountainous regions, deserts and forests, where equipment developed for other countries might not be suitable.

But he acknowledged that this technology was still at an early stage.

Experience developing drones and robots for India's diverse terrain could also help manufacturers expand into overseas markets with similar conditions.

For instance, IdeaForge has used its drones for high-altitude mapping in the Himalayas and demonstrated their ability to operate in Alaska's freezing conditions to US defence customers, according to its FY2023-24 annual report.

The United States is among IdeaForge's priority overseas markets. The company said in its annual report that it had secured its first US order from a police department in Texas and formed a partnership to explore opportunities in Japan.

'NOBODY IS GOING TO HELP US WHEN THE CHIPS ARE DOWN'

Despite growing military demand, India's drone industry faces challenges including reliance on imported components and difficulties deploying new technologies, said experts.

Hari Kumar R, director of research and development at state-owned Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), said India had made progress in developing electronic components domestically, but advanced infrared sensors used for night-time military surveillance remained difficult to source.

Speaking at a panel discussion at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, he stressed the need to develop local alternatives and diversify suppliers to prevent disruptions caused by shortages or foreign restrictions.

“Nobody is going to help us when the chips are down. Each country stands up to itself,” he said.

B.K. Das, a senior official at India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), also flagged reliance on imported materials, including rare earth magnets used in drone motors.

“[The challenge is] we do research in isolation,” he told CNA, calling for greater collaboration among India's research institutions, startups and defence companies to develop advanced military systems.

Das said DRDO had established 15 centres at universities and research institutions to help bridge that gap.

Das acknowledged that emerging technologies still needed further development to meet stringent military standards, including the ability to withstand harsh weather, equipment failures and other challenging conditions.

Meanwhile, securing a predictable flow of military orders remains another challenge for Indian startups operating in the space.

Citing Ministry of Defence figures, Kohli said 45 procurement contracts worth about 23.3 billion Indian rupees had been signed under the government's iDEX initiative as of February.

“Revenue is real now, but much of it is still lumpy,” Kohli said, referring to the irregular flow of orders and income for defence startups.

She said emergency military purchases had helped some companies secure business, but sporadic orders made it difficult for startups to plan long-term investments, expand production and retain skilled workers.

“A startup cannot hire engineers or build a factory on orders that arrive in bursts,” she said.

Kohli added that more predictable procurement, stronger domestic supply chains and manufacturing capabilities would be key to building a sustainable defence-tech industry in India.

“The market becomes sustainable when one-time buys turn into multi-year orders,” she said.

articles.body:
A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.

Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.

“He has been repeatedly abusive and insulting to Canadians,” May said as she formally introduced the petition, according to Politico.

She called Donald Trump’s envoy “the most undiplomatic diplomat” Canada had ever seen.

The petition accuses Hoekstra of “undermining” Canada-US diplomatic relations through repeated statements about Canadian politics that its signatories say are “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol”.

The US state department said it was aware of the petition.

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particularly for his response to Trump’s desire to annex the country and make Canada the 51st US state.

Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the president’s rhetoric as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”.

Hoekstra also previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election that saw a remarkable come-from-behind victory for the prime minister’s Liberal party as “anti-American”.

The US ambassador had suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans performed poorly in this month’s midterm elections.

“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney replied, when asked about the comments.

Democrats swept the November elections, including key Senate races in border states such as Michigan and Maine, where the bitter tariff war between Washington and Ottawa has hit residents hard.

Last month Carney said American tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.

“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”

Hoekstra had also accused Canada of potential “political interference” in the US election, a claim Carney said held “no merit”. Speaking to reporters in Turkey, the prime minister said he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.

Even though the Canadian government is required to provide a formal response to the petition presented by May, the petition is nonbinding.

“I think the government will quite likely say, ‘No, we’re not prepared to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata and strip him of his diplomatic credentials,’”, May said in an interview with CTV.

Despite this possibility, May expects the petition to signal to Trump that the Canadian government has the support of its constituents, and she hopes the government can use it as leverage against Trump with Democrats holding power in Congress for the second half of Trump’s term.

articles.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
articles.summary: Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
articles.preview: November 27, 2026 Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights. Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants. However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.
articles.body:
November 27, 2026

Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

What did the Supreme Court say about the law?

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."

Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections

Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

articles.body:
Four of Khalil al-Hayya’s other sons were previously killed by Israeli forces, according to the Palestinian group.

A son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya has survived an Israeli air strike targeting his family in Gaza, said the Palestinian group.

The air raid on Friday came as Israeli attacks elsewhere in the strip killed four Palestinians, despite the so-called “ceasefire” agreed over a year ago.

Izzeldeen al-Hayya, 29, and his family survived the Israeli strike at dawn, said Hamas official Basem Naim. Hamas sources told the Reuters news agency that several relatives were wounded, including the daughter-in-law of the Hamas chief.

The family of another of Khalil al-Hayya’s deceased sons, Azzam, also survived.

Naim described Izzeldeen as the Hamas leader’s last surviving son. Four of his brothers were killed by Israeli forces: Hamza in 2008, Osama in 2014, Humam in September last year and Azzam in May this year.

Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Humam, who was killed in an Israeli strike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last year. Khalil al-Hayya narrowly escaped that attack during negotiations. He was named leader of Hamas in July.

Hamas condemned Friday’s attack, describing it as an attempt to “assassinate” al-Hayya’s son and target his family.

The group linked the attack to threats made against its leader by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and accused Israel of seeking to undermine the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. Hamas said the “cowardly act” exposes the “complete detachment from human and moral values” of Israeli leaders.

Continued Israeli attacks in Gaza

Deadly Israeli attacks continued elsewhere in Gaza on Friday.

A Palestinian was killed and several others wounded in a drone att on a vehicle in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency.

Wafa named the victim as Khaled Assaf and quoted witnesses as saying a vehicle was struck in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp.

In the southern city of Rafah, Civil Defence teams recovered the bodies of three Palestinians and rescued two wounded people following an attack near Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, Wafa reported.

Israeli army gunfire injured a Palestinian child in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.

Medical sources and witnesses told Wafa that Israeli forces repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced people in the area from their positions near the eastern “Yellow Line”.

Friday’s attacks followed a series of Israeli raids on Thursday that killed 10 Palestinians, including a senior education official.

Israel’s ‘incitement against hospitals’

Also on Friday, Hamas described as “ridiculous” the Israeli army’s claim that it used one of the buildings at Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital in Gaza City as an interrogation centre.

The Israeli military and Shin Bet made the allegations on Thursday, claiming Hamas was conducting military activities within the hospital complex.

The Israeli claim “comes as part of the ongoing incitement against hospitals in the Gaza Strip”, Hamas said in a statement.

Hospitals are “public places open to all civil and UN institutions operating in the enclave”, it noted, adding that Israel had never provided evidence to substantiate any of its claims.

The Episcopal Diocese of Jerusalem, which oversees the hospital, said it had no knowledge of any secret interrogation centre on the premises.

According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the October 2025 “ceasefire” since it took effect have killed at least 1,705 Palestinians and wounded 6,163. Israel has killed at least 74,772 Palestinians in Gaza since the genocidal war began in October 2023.

articles.preview: Department for Work and Pensions urges people to be alert to scams related to outage and contact helpline with urgent difficulties Tell us: have you been affected by the DWP ‘cyber incident’ Benefits and pensions claimants have faced chaos after the system was hit by a “serious cyber incident”, fuelling concerns about the UK government’s ability to defend itself against malicious attacks.
articles.body:
Benefits and pensions claimants have faced chaos after the system was hit by a “serious cyber incident”, fuelling concerns about the UK government’s ability to defend itself against malicious attacks.

The government took its portal down late on Thursday after detecting “unusual activity”, meaning anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit on Friday was unable to do so.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said all regular benefit payments were still being made but many claimants said they were worried about delays in applying for emergency payments, had seen their appointments cancelled and were unable to access their accounts.

The incident comes days after the government issued a warning of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks in the UK, particularly against businesses supporting Ukraine.

Downing Street has not ruled out that a “malicious” actor was behind the incident, but said there was no evidence that customer data had been lost or that any other departments had been targeted.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) urged people to be alert to any scams related to the outage and stressed that the government would never ask people to confirm bank details or click a link. It also said people should contact their benefit helpline if they were having urgent difficulties and confirmed that no one would face a sanction for not meeting conditions while the system was offline.

DWP insiders said payments for Friday would already have been sent earlier in the week, but there could be a backlog of manual payments running into tens of thousands due early next week to be processed over the weekend. Internal DWP systems were restored on Friday, allowing officials to begin working again, but the public-facing portal remained offline.

The cause of the incident is not publicly known but GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre is investigating, indicating there is a suspicion it may have been malicious activity.

Senior MPs called for the government to redouble its efforts to protect its systems. Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons science and technology committee, said it should be a “wake-up call” for the government and public bodies.

She said: “People rely on these systems for some of the most essential services the state provides, and they should be able to trust that the tech and data underpinning them are secure and resilient.

“My committee has repeatedly warned that the government cannot achieve its digital transformation of public services without addressing weaknesses in its digital infrastructure and improving standards of data hygiene. Public bodies hold citizens’ data on trust, and that demands the highest standards.”

Ben Spencer, the Conservative shadow AI minister, said the cyber incident was “deeply concerning and highlights once again why the security of government systems cannot be taken for granted”.

He said: “I and colleagues have repeatedly warned about potential vulnerabilities in government technology and called for greater transparency and scrutiny of the action being taken to modernise outdated systems and strengthen cybersecurity.”

McFadden said there was a “constant effort” to ensure systems were secure. “When an incident like this happens, the most important thing is to take the system offline as early as possible to protect it, then to investigate the causes, and at the same time to make sure that payments to the public can continue as normal.”

The disruption caused concern among the public, with some reporting problems. One woman who has two young children told BBC Radio 4 that she normally received a universal credit payment on the 27th day of each month and, like others, was concerned about not having enough money to cover bills due to be paid on 1 December.

“It’s a bit scary because when I called them [the DWP] to ask, they said they couldn’t give me any other information other than the payment would definitely be made by Monday,” she said.

“My weekly shop is on a Sunday so I am having to go into Christmas savings, which I have been saving for the last six or seven months. I am having to pull money out of them to make up for what I don’t have and there are bills coming out also next week.”

Sarah Merritt, a 23-year-old graduate, said her JobCentre appointment was cancelled because of the outages. “I get to my appointment only to hear all appointments are cancelled because of the cyber-attacks – as all services went offline, people with appointments were not able to be informed. This means I had to walk there and back in the rain for no reason. Although I know it’s not the staff’s fault, you would hope that these situations would be better prevented.”

Wilf Frith, 64, another claimant, said he could not access a video call for a standard work search review after he requested to cancel his claim due to finding more work.

“I haven’t heard anything from DWP, and usually if I were to miss an appointment they’d send a message within minutes like ‘where are you’,” he said. “My condition is better than that of many, as I’m moving away from being in need of support, but a lot of people are in need and their whole job search will be slowed up because of this incident and they might be missing opportunities.”

The department said in a statement: “We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems. We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and government cyber coordination centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.

“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.”

The DWP’s most senior official told a committee of MPs this month that cybersecurity and resilience was one of the issues “that keeps a new permanent secretary awake”.

Sarah Healey, the DWP permanent secretary, was appearing before the work and pensions select committee, where she was asked who would ensure that DWP systems would “not be the frontline in some sort of hybrid warfare from the Kremlin”.

Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned earlier this month, with thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F), in what was blamed on a cyber-attack. The EU condemned the “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

Burundi

Burundi's electoral commission on Friday rejected an application from the country's main opposition leader to contest in the presidential polls next year. President Evariste Ndayishimiye will seek a second term in the May 3 general elections for the ruling CNDD-FDD party, which has been in power since 2005 and is widely considered the favourite. Agathon Rwasa, an ex-militia leader who fought in the country's civil war, lost to Ndayishimiye in 2020's polls, which the opposition labelled an "electoral charade".

The electoral commission said Rwasa had made a "false declaration" in his application, as he had registered as an independent candidate despite remaining a member of a political party. "Consequently, the Independent National Electoral Commission rejects his candidacy," according to an official document seen by AFP. The commission approved seven out of 10 applicants, and those rejected have two days to challenge the decision before the Constitutional Court.

The final list of candidates will be published on December 6. Rwasa's disqualification came as "no surprise" to prominent exiled civil society activist Pacifique Nininahazwe. "It concludes a process of political elimination initiated by the regime of Évariste Ndayishimiye... to neutralise his primary rival," he told AFP. Burundi is one of the world's poorest countries and has a history of deadly political crises and a civil war that killed around 300,000 people between 1993 and 2005. Earlier this month, Ndayishimiye submitted his candidacy papers, paying a deposit of 100 million Burundian francs ($33,000).

Opposition parties argue the huge sum imposed by the authorities is designed to prevent them from participating in the election. The president's CNDD-FDD party won all 100 seats in the 2025 National Assembly elections -- which also saw irregularities. Ndayishimiye has led Burundi since June 2020 after the death of his iron-fisted predecessor, Pierre Nkurunziza, who ruled for 15 years.

Since then, the former Belgian colony has swung between signs of liberalising a government still in thrall to the country's powerful generals and cracking down on the opposition. Both rights groups and the United Nations have criticised breaches of human rights in the country. In October, the UN Human Rights Council expressed concern over an "alarming increase in extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances".

articles.title: UN rights chief voices concern as Costa Rica bars Francesca Albanese
articles.summary: UN rights chief voices concern as Costa Rica bars Francesca Albanese Costa Rica denied entry to Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, drawing criticism from UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday. Turk said he was "deeply concerned" by Costa Rica's decision to bar Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital San Jose. Albanese, an Italian national, had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica. The UN human rights office said on X that Albanese was denied entry on "claimed national security grounds". The government of Costa Rica asserted that Albanese was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts". An Italian lawyer, Albanese is the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory, which has been occupied by Israel since 1967. She has been sanctioned by the United States since 2025. "I am deeply indignant that the government of Costa Rica has spread false information that links me to terrorism," Albanese said from the airport, adding that she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision. Israel's UN ambassador, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica's decision in a post on X. Under President Laura Fernandez, Costa Rica has deepened cooperation with the United States on security and moved closer to Israel. It signed a free trade agreement with Israel last year. articles.summary: Canada's Supreme Court upholds law banning hijabs in Quebec public sector Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Fri, 11/27/2026 - 16:11 The country's former and only Islamophobia envoy calls the decision "devastating" A view of the exterior of the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa, Ontario, on 12 July 2017 (Creative Commons) Off The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday upheld Quebec's highly contested 2019 law that bans religious symbols in the public sector. It was, more than anything, seen to be targeting Muslim women in the province who wear the hijab, but also impacted Catholics, Sikhs and other minorities. Quebec's population is 5 percent Muslim , according to the last census carried out in 2021. That figure is second only to Ontario. Amira Elghawaby, who was Canada’s first and only special representative on combatting Islamophobia, until her office was shut down earlier this year, called the verdict "devastating". "The promise of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been broken, and could be broken again and again. It means that religious freedoms, equality and the rights of all Canadians are no longer guaranteed," Elghawaby said in a statement released by the organisation she founded this year, the Muslim Communities Research Observatory. “This ruling will instantly further impact the lives and livelihoods of Quebecers, particularly Muslim women who wear the hijab. In one study, 71% of Muslim women surveyed had considered leaving Quebec, with the province standing to lose an estimated $3.2 billion in income. It may also open the door for further violations of rights and freedoms," she added. Technicality Oftentimes rulings by the highest court come down to technicalities. What the court was looking at in this case was the application of Section 33 of the constitution, known as the "notwithstanding clause", which shields Bill 21 from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms itself. US midterm elections 2026: Record number of hijabis elected to statewide and national offices  to invoke. Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said in 2022 that Canada's charter "cannot become a suggestion". The Canadian Department of Justice acknowledges that it is a "unique" provision among constitutional democracies, because it allows the Canadian parliament or a provincial legislature "to derogate from certain sections of the Charter, namely section 2 (fundamental freedoms), sections 7 to 14 (legal rights) and section 15 (equality rights)". Section 333 does not apply to voting, mobility or language rights. articles.title: Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit
articles.summary: An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.
articles.preview: November 27, 2026 An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds. EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.
articles.body:
November 27, 2026

An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.

EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.

Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.

There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.

"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.

The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.

Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."

Germany demands more for competitiveness, security, defense

Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.

Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."

As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.

In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).

"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."

Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.

"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.

Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.

Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.

They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.

In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.

EU looking elsewhere to raise funds

The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.

The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.

But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.

"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.

Protecting the EU's top triple-A rating

There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.

The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.

EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."

Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.

"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."

Enache called the tax proposal "politically impossible."

EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.

articles.preview: Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator paints Russian invasion of Ukraine as a misunderstanding to be resolved In the space of a 70-minute interview, Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a prominent US negotiator in Russia, Gaza and Iran – probably did more to reveal why the world is mired in entrenched conflicts than a thousand geopolitical tomes or seminars.
articles.body:
In the space of a 70-minute interview, Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a prominent US negotiator in Russia, Gaza and Iran – probably did more to reveal why the world is mired in entrenched conflicts than a thousand geopolitical tomes or seminars.

During the conversation this week with Mathias Döpfner, the chief executive of the Axel Springer media publisher, Kushner gave a rare insight into his diplomatic technique, offering a string of homilies that veered close to banalities: “You have nothing until you have something”, “diplomacy is like untying knots on a fishing line for his son”, and “you play the ball from where it lands”.

There were also many happy admissions of historical ignorance. Since taking on the Ukraine brief a year ago, Kushner said, he had to learn “the algorithm of Europe and how complicated that is”, and he had to get abreast of “the local issues with Ukraine”.

As a businessman he brought a special expertise, he claimed. “Look at what’s happening in the Middle East with sanctions, with Russia, with Iran. I think that you have to understand economics in order to understand geopolitics because the two go together very, very closely,” he said.

But the main revelation was how much he believes the Ukraine conflict is not a case of an aggressor and a victim – but is simply a series of misunderstandings and miscommunication.

Indeed, he treated Vladimir Putin as if he were a masterful corporate executive quite willing to close the deal if he were only given the right economic incentives – instead of a man ready to sacrifice hundreds of thousands of Russians to reclaim part of a historical empire.

In the process, Kushner revealed – often inadvertently – that he had largely bought into the Russian narrative of a string of postwar missteps by Europe and the US coming to a head in Nato’s expansion eastwards after 9/11.

That, in turn, has led him to adopt Moscow’s central demand to reshape the European security order to allow Russia, without opprobrium, to retain land it has gained by force. Shining through his answers was a naive bias towards the aggressor, presented as a mediator’s desire to understand both parties.

Praise veering on awe for the Russian leader flowed. “Putin – people can like what he has done, they can not like what he has done – [but] he is a grand master of politics. He is a historic figure,” he said. Any sense that Putin may have blundered escaped him.

As to the rights and wrongs of invading another country, Kushner was blasé. “After all, most lines in Europe have changed over time and they are decided through war or peace, or concessions. It’s not about fairness or who is right or wrong. It’s about ending the killing,” he said.

He understood, too, why Putin could not offer a ceasefire: “He has very little confidence that if he stops the war, that he [will] be able to get to a postwar settlement that leads to not having a future war.”

To stop the killing, the killing has to go on.

What is more, Kushner was struck by the Russian leader’s self-control. “So far Putin has shown restraint and he has agreed not to use nuclear weapons and he has reassured us that is his intention.”

Kushner denied Trump had put any pressure on Volodymyr Zelenskyy, defying his interviewer to provide evidence – at which point Döpfner recited a list of examples, including only last month when the US president suggested that Ukraine should get a new leader.

Trump was “a strong counter-puncher”, argued Kushner, implying that Zelenskyy had thrown the first punch in a conflict that began with a Russian invasion. Relations with Ukraine were cooperative, he said before pointedly saying Kyiv needed things from the US, without which “Ukraine will not be safe in the future”.

After noting that “the territorial issue is now a little bit of a deadlock”, his strategic insight was that if a future security architecture for Europe could be agreed, the answer to the land question in Donbas would eventually follow.

In essence, he proposed a revival of the Russia-Nato council, one of the bodies eviscerated by Putin’s war.

He also envisioned Ukraine inside the European Union with security guarantees akin to those offered by Nato’s article five. Though it was impossible at this stage to give “more specificity” about these guarantees in the detailed way Ukraine sought, he admitted.

So far, neither Moscow nor Kyiv have bought this plan, let alone a wary Europe.

Kushner tried to be polite about Europe, insisting it had to be at the negotiating table, but he could not stop himself characterising European military assistance to Ukraine as a “proxy war” against Russia.

As an analysis of why the Ukraine war had not ended inside the 24 hours Trump had promised when he took office again, Kushner showed an alarming belief that the answer lay in granting more concessions to Putin, and that the misunderstandings and misperceptions would then evaporate.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau's military government defends postponement of elections
articles.summary: The presidency said there were insufficient "technical, material, and financial conditions" to organise a credible vote as planned in December.
articles.preview: Guinea-Bissau Guinea-Bissau has defended its decision to postpone next month’s planned presidential and legislative elections until 2028. Its military leaders on Thursday said conditions were not in place to hold the polls and stick to the one-year transition to civilian rule promised after last year’s coup. Transitional president, General Horta N'Tam, said government of the country has been assured at all levels in the current “special context”.
articles.body:
Guinea-Bissau

Guinea-Bissau has defended its decision to postpone next month’s planned presidential and legislative elections until 2028.

Its military leaders on Thursday said conditions were not in place to hold the polls and stick to the one-year transition to civilian rule promised after last year’s coup.

Transitional president, General Horta N'Tam, said government of the country has been assured at all levels in the current “special context”.

"Internationally, Guinea-Bissau has managed to preserve a good level of relations with its bilateral and multilateral partners,” he added.

N’Tam said the behaviour of Guineans over the period had been “marked by civility and respect for the authorities” and he hoped it would stay that way.

The presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material, and financial conditions" to organise a credible vote.

Regional bloc ECOWAS had called for a short, structured, and transparent transition back to civilian rule after the ousting of President Umaro Sissoco Embalo.

The elections will now be held on 26 November 2028, three years after the generals came to power.

N'Tam said there was a need to "institutionalise local authorities" by holding the country's first-ever municipal elections, he added.

In an address to the nation Thursday evening on national television, N'Tam described the transition record to date as "positive".

He said a nationwide electoral census would have to be carried out with new mapping drawn up "according to the new division of electoral constituencies, which will go from 29 to 12".

N’Tam also said the number of members of parliament would be reduced from 102 to 65.

The reforms needed to address these challenges required more time and more resources than initially planned, he said.

The military coup on 26 November 2025 came on the eve of the scheduled announcement of provisional results for the presidential and legislative elections held three days earlier.

Incumbent president Umaro Sissoco Embalo was overthrown and the electoral process was suspended.

The military government held a constitutional referendum in August that replaced the semi-parliamentary structure with strengthened presidential powers. The opposition had called for a boycott of the vote.

Many observers suspected Embalo of orchestrating the 2025 coup to halt an election process he appeared to be losing.

However, the current leadership has more recently taken several steps suggesting it is distancing itself from the former president.

The Portuguese-speaking country has seen four previous coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Lisbon in 1974.

articles.title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
articles.summary: France's president made the comment while speaking to French farming representatives, months after the EU banned Brazil beef and poultry products.
articles.preview: Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron calling Brazilian meat "doped". France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry, which took effect in September. The Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".
articles.body:
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron calling Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry, which took effect in September.

The Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.

Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".

Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.
