articles.title: China and Belt and Road partners step up cooperation on green energy
articles.summary: Energy cooperation is taking centre stage as Belt and Road countries push for a greener, more secure global energy future. Ministers wrapped up the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministerial Conference in Qingdao, eastern China.
articles.preview: China Energy ministers from Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) participating countries have stressed the importance of cooperation in advancing green transition and safeguarding energy security across the globe. These priorities took center stage as the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministerial Conference wrapped up in east China's Qingdao on Friday. Held under the theme "Sharing innovation outcomes, advancing energy transition, building a secure future together," the two-day event brought officials together to translate those goals into action.
articles.body:
China

Energy ministers from Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) participating countries have stressed the importance of cooperation in advancing green transition and safeguarding energy security across the globe.

These priorities took center stage as the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministerial Conference wrapped up in east China's Qingdao on Friday. Held under the theme "Sharing innovation outcomes, advancing energy transition, building a secure future together," the two-day event brought officials together to translate those goals into action.

Discussions centered on innovation-driven energy transition, energy security and system resilience, and coordinated efforts toward a green, low-carbon transition across industrial and supply chains. During the conference, Wang Hongzhi, administrator of the National Energy Administration of China, said China is accelerating its new energy system. By 2030, China aims for a cleaner, low-carbon system, with a better energy mix, stronger resilience and more innovation.

"Kazakhstan is a big new exporter of the hydrocarbons to the Chinese market. The energy sector is the fundamental of our cooperation. We built a lot of projects in the renewable energy, in the processing of the raw materials. Chinese companies are taking a lot of works in Kazakhstan in building the energy infrastructure," said Yerlan Akkenzhenov, Minister of Energy of Kazakhstan.

"We think that China is leading the way to the transformation, that is sharing the advancement and the technology, also enhancing the cooperation between the members of the [Belt and Road] Initiative," said Al-Mutasim Ibrahim, Minister of Energy and Petroleum of Republic of Sudan.

The conference released a Blue Book on green, low-carbon transition and security resilience in developing countries. The Blue Book sets up a four-dimensional evaluation system and classifies developing countries into 16 energy-system types, offering tailored solutions in technology, policy, finance and smart digitalization.

"There is no single model for the energy transition. Countries need to set roadmaps based on their own conditions, balancing green and low-carbon goals, energy security, system resilience and economic affordability. In terms of the international cooperation, the Blue Book recommends expanding from project construction alone to broader areas such as planning consultation, standards alignment, digital and intelligent empowerment, and risk resilience enhancement, helping countries turn resource advantages into momentum for sustainable development," said Zhou Yi, director of China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute.

"New energy here is everywhere. Every household, when I go out of the big cities, I see even the farmers installing solar panels on their house, because now it's just basically cheaper. They are not only installing to use for themselves. They also sell it to grid. So basically, they earn money by using their roof. That's amazing," said Rafael Bekshentayev, head representative in China of EXia Energy Research Center, a Kazakhstan-based energy analytics, and research organization.

The conference also saw the formally established of the Governing Board of Belt and Road Energy Partnership, a multilateral energy cooperation platform under the BRI. The Belt and Road Energy Partnership has expanded to 35 BRI member countries, with its cooperation network bringing together nearly 300 enterprises.

articles.title: L’inverno alle porte
articles.summary: La neve è tornata a imbiancare le Alpi. Nei prossimi giorni le temperature scenderanno in tutta l’Italia
articles.preview: La neve è tornata a imbiancare le Alpi. Il passaggio di alcune perturbazioni atlantiche ha portato ancora piogge e forti mareggiate lungo le coste tirreniche, mentre il progressivo calo delle temperature ha permesso alla neve di scendere copiosa fino ai 1.500 metri di quota, dal Piemonte alle montagne del Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Gli accumuli più consistenti (30-40 centimetri) sono stati misurati sulle Alpi occidentali di confine e sulle Dolomiti.

Il passaggio di alcune perturbazioni atlantiche ha portato ancora piogge e forti mareggiate lungo le coste tirreniche, mentre il progressivo calo delle temperature ha permesso alla neve di scendere copiosa fino ai 1.500 metri di quota, dal Piemonte alle montagne del Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Gli accumuli più consistenti (30-40 centimetri) sono stati misurati sulle Alpi occidentali di confine e sulle Dolomiti.

articles.summary: The US military says it disabled the Palau-flagged ship’s propulsion but its crew was unharmed.
articles.preview: The US military says it disabled the Palau-flagged ship’s propulsion but its crew was unharmed. The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports. Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the “ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed”, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement.
articles.body:
The US military says it disabled the Palau-flagged ship’s propulsion but its crew was unharmed.

The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports.

Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the “ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed”, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement.

US officials say the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel’s destination as Singapore. It is at least the 15th vessel the US military has publicly acknowledged disabling since the blockade began in April, and the sixth since it resumed it in July. The previous vessel was disabled on November 7.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an “unauthorised” route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.

The claims could not be independently verified.

The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said on Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations “that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region’s waters”.

American blockade action

The US military has maintained a sizeable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.

American ships have been blockading Iranian ports since April, although the blockade was temporarily lifted during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the US military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabled those that refuse to comply.

CENTCOM, which has its headquarters in Florida, has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.

articles.title: Several Palestinians beaten and detained in Israeli raids across occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Several Palestinians beaten and detained in Israeli raids across occupied West Bank Raids and attacks by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank on Friday left at least three Palestinians injured and several detained. Three Palestinians were injured and another, identified as Muhammad Daifallah Arara, was detained on Friday night after Israeli occupation forces raided his home north of occupied Jerusalem and assaulted those inside. The three sustained injuries to their shoulders, limbs and abdomens after being beaten by Israeli soldiers, according to the Jerusalem Governorate. Earlier, a group of Israeli settlers attacked the family's home, attempting to break down its entrance and storm its courtyard, before Israeli forces intervened and raided the house. Israeli forces raided a residential cave in the village of Khirbet Khallat al-Daba'a in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, on Friday evening, assaulting its owner, detaining his family members and vandalising property inside, Wafa news agency reported. The cave belongs to activist Jaber al-Dababseh, who was beaten by Israeli soldiers while his family members were detained. On Friday evening, Israeli forces fired tear gas at Palestinian residents in the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, during a raid. Israeli soldiers forced shop owners to close their stores. In the village of Jayyus, east of Qalqilya, Israeli forces detained seven Palestinians after raiding their homes and ransacking their property. Israeli settlers also continued their attacks across the occupied West Bank throughout the day. They attacked Palestinian vehicles in the Wadi al-Shaer area in the Salfit governorate, damaging at least two, locals told Wafa. In the town of Za'tara, east of Bethlehem, settlers set up tents, raising fears among Palestinian residents that they could pave the way for a new Israeli outpost there. Separately, a group of Israeli settlers dumped waste near a Palestinian home in the Turmus Ayya Plain, north of Ramallah. articles.title: Oman's stock market on track to beat all Gulf states in 2026
articles.summary: Oman's stock market on track to beat all Gulf states in 2026 Submitted by Sean Mathews on Fri, 11/27/2026 - 21:00 Oman's economy has emerged as a relative winner amid the Iran war thanks to its geography and diplomacy, experts say A man views Rasool al-Adham Mosque from the corniche at Port Sultan Qaboos in Oman's capital, Muscat, on 5 February 2026 (Loic Venance/AFP) Off Oman’s stock market is on track to be the best performer in the Gulf region in 2026, with its economic growth pulling ahead of neighbours, in a sign of how it is reaping gains from distancing itself from the US-Israeli war on Iran. The MSX30 Index, which tracks the performance of Oman’s stock exchange, has soared 22 percent year-to-date. Dubai's stock market, the Dubai Financial Market General Index, the region’s second-best performer, is up 8.7 percent year-to-date. Saudi Arabia’s Tadawul market is down 3 percent year-to-date. For comparison, in the US, the SP500 index is up 6.4 percent year-to-date after a sharp selloff in AI and technology. Both the Saudi and Dubai stock markets have clawed back the steep losses of earlier this year after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran. But Oman's success is more interesting when one considers the anger US President Donald Trump directed at it during negotiations with Iran over the way to manage traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which is comprised of Iran and Oman's territorial waters. Trump threatened to “blow up” Oman, where his family real estate business has licensed its name for use on a golf resort. Oman: From outlier to trailblazer Tensions are still simmering between the US and Iran. The US has launched strikes on Iran and its vessels, while Iran has attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf countries. Kuwait blamed Iran for a strike on Thursday that killed two Italian soldiers at a military site. Iran denied responsibility, but in recent weeks has launched strikes on Kuwait and Bahrain, both of which host US military bases. 'From outlier to trailblazer': How Oman offers a glimpse into the post-war Gulf  in the Iran war, experts say. Middle East Eye reported in June that Oman’s geography, diplomacy and business acumen would put it at the forefront of a new order emerging in the Gulf where Iran is emboldened and the US’s security umbrella clouded by distrust. Muscat was a mediator between Tehran and Washington in the months before the war. Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi made a rare public plea for diplomacy just before the US-Israeli attack, which was ignored in Washington. Despite lobbying against the war, in relative terms, Oman is attracting more interest from investors and companies as they look for a safe haven that has not come under intense Iranian attack. Geography and US bases Oman also sits outside the Strait of Hormuz and boasts a large Indian Ocean coastline. Oman’s two main ports experienced an unprecedented surge in traffic during the war. Sohar port saw a 1,766 percent surge in ship destination change requests in March, while Salalah saw an 800 percent increase, according to maritime intelligence firm Windward. 'Vulnerability exposed': War on Iran will change how the US bases troops in Gulf s like Saudi Arabia. One of the most obvious reasons Oman has not borne the brunt of Iranian strikes is its decision not to join the US and Israel in attacking Tehran. It also has a different approach to basing the US military, which resembles that of some European countries. Oman is the US’s oldest treaty partner in the Gulf, going back to 1833. But Oman hosts no permanent US military facilities or troops, unlike Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Instead, the US has an “access agreement” to use Omani ports. Albusaidi said earlier this year that the US was pursuing the war on Iran in the interest of Israel, and that Iran’s strikes on Gulf states hosting US military bases were ”inevitable”. The International Monetary Fund estimates Iran’s economy to grow 4 percent this year, whereas every other Gulf economy is expected to contract, with the GCC overall shrinking 4.8 percent. articles.summary: CCTV shows unidentified woman taking scissors to Middlesbrough home’s festive display An elderly woman has been accused of defying the season of goodwill after appearing to cut down her neighbour’s Christmas lights. CCTV footage showed her approaching a property on a mobility scooter brandishing scissors. Continue reading...

articles.body:
An elderly woman has been accused of defying the season of goodwill after appearing to cut down her neighbour’s Christmas lights.

CCTV footage showed her approaching a property on a mobility scooter brandishing scissors.

After several seconds, the Christmas lights at Beth Wilson-Croft’s house in Middlesbrough, North Yorkshire, which is surrounded by lights with an inflatable Father Christmas and Rudolph on the roof and two snowmen in the garden, went out.

The woman then fled the scene on her scooter at about 11pm on Wednesday.

Wilson-Croft said most of her neighbours enjoyed her festive display and she had never seen the alleged perpetrator before, the Daily Mail reported.

The 31-year-old said she had reported the vandalism to the police.

In an effort to find the woman, Wilson-Croft posted the footage online and wrote: “If you don’t like my Christmas decorations that’s an absolute shame for you because they’ll be back up today alongside a singing Santa and a snow machine and anything else I can get my hands on.”

After seeing the video of the incident, a man offered to help and fixed the lights by soldering them back together.

Wilson-Croft, who has a six-year-old child, has subsequently shared photographs showing her lights restored.

The footage triggered outrage from neighbours who accused the perpetrator of flouting the festive spirit and described her as a “Grinch” and a “Scrooge”.

The family’s seasonal decorations draw visitors from around the area.

articles.body:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Surviving blackouts

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

Raving through the war

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% â way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method â sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia â "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a cafÃ© here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.

articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

- Published7 days ago

- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

- Published6 days ago

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Tough winter

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.body:
The proposal comes as President Zelenskyy criticises Trump’s ‘friendship’ with Putin.

Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.

“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.

Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.

He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.

Previous attempts at a ceasefire

The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters, and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.

A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.

In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.

International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.

On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.

Friends to foes

The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.

In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.

“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.

He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.

“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.

After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.

Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

articles.body:
'I can’t conceive of us losing,' Sánchez says despite adverse polling

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported.

Amid a legal ban on publishing new opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.

“I can’t conceive of us losing,” Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.

However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today – but join us on Sunday night for the Spanish election night!

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote (12:39).

Current polling shows that once-mocked far-right Vox party, now the third largest party in Spain, is poised to pick up almost 20% of the voteand, very possibly, to form a coalition government with the conservative People’s party (16:27).

Last night’s final TV debate saw Ada Colau, the leader of the leftwing Broad Front, come out on top, with People party’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo coming under fire for what critics said were his “sexist” comments towards the former Barcelona mayor (11:52).

The main parties are set to hold their closing rallies this evening, with the Socialists and the Broad Front choosing Madrid for their events. The PP and Vox have opted for Seville and Valencia (14:40).

On Saturday, Spaniards observe a “day of reflection” on the eve of the vote. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.

I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.

Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government? - explainer

Sam Jones

in Madrid

Spaniards head to the polls on 29 November to vote in the country’s sixth general election in 11 years.

The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government for the first time since Spain’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Franco.

Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s socialist prime minister, called the snap election on 5 October after the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party and the rightwing, pro-independence Catalan party Junts voted down emergency measures the government had put together to tackle a housing crisis.

The lack of affordable housing has become a key electoral issue, triggering large protests across Spain. The issue was thrown into sharp relief by the case of the late Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment. More than 3 million people took part in a recent general strike called in response to soaring housing prices.

Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) are hoping their efforts to address the housing crisis – and the fact their plans were torpedoed by the PP, Vox and Junts – will mobilise progressive voters and deliver them another four-year term.

But it is a risky strategy.

All the polls point to the PP finishing first in the election but falling short of an absolute majority. That means it would need to enlist the support of Vox to help it govern. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would signal the return of the far right to government in Spain for the first time in the country’s post-dictatorship democratic history.

From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes

Sam Jones

in Madrid

Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain.

The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil.

Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.

Until that moment, the prevailing wisdom had been that Spain’s experiences of the Franco dictatorship had inoculated the country against the far right, and that Vox was a tiny, fringe outfit whose prospects were terminally limited after it had picked up just 0.2% of the vote in the 2016 general election.

Fast-forward to late 2026 and the horseman seems less comical still. Vox, now the third largest party in Spain, is poised to pick up almost 20% of the vote in the snap general election on 29 Novemberand, very possibly, to form a coalition government with the conservative People’s party (PP).

Spain’s election: the end of a leftwing icon? - podcast

He has become an icon of the European left. A great political survivor, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez has been in power for eight years while – across the continent – the right has been on the march.

The Socialist party leader has championed immigration, stood up to Donald Trump and been a notable voice for Palestinians in Gaza.

But on Sunday, Sánchez might be replaced by a conservative government in league with the far right.

Madrid correspondent Sam Jones and European community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam report on a pivotal Spanish election, and the gamble that led Sánchez to call it.

Where will this leave the left in Spain, asks Nosheen Iqbal, and across Europe too?

Norse Atlantic budget carrier files for bankruptcy

In other news, budget carrier Norse Atlantic said on Friday it would file a petition for bankruptcy for its main Norwegian operating unit, becoming the latest airline to succumb to soaring fuel costs wrought by the war in Iran.

“Norse Atlantic has stopped flying. All flights operated by Norse Atlantic Airways AS and Norse Atlantic UK Ltd from 27 November at 14.00 CET are cancelled. This includes return flights. Please do not go to the airport for a cancelled flight,” the company said in a statement on its website.

The airline failed to pay its employees’ November salaries this week, a pilot union said Thursday, as reported by AFP.

Norse is the second European airline to enter bankruptcy proceedings this year after Latvia’s airBaltic, highlighting the toll of the Iran war on carriers that entered the crisis without fuel hedges as jet fuel prices surged, Reuters noted.

The company said it had not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs, with the board deciding to file a bankruptcy petition on 27 November with the Agder District Court in Norway for its operating subsidiary.

Will Spain’s housing crisis bring the far right to power? – video

As mass protests over a nationwide housing crisis have forced Sánchez into an early general election, the Guardian travelled to Spain’s Andalusian coast to find out what’s driving the housing crisis, what solutions are on offer and why rightwing populists are gaining ground.

In Spain, the parties are set to hold their closing rallies this evening, with the Socialists and the Broad Front choosing Madrid for their events.

Meanwhile, the PP and Vox have opted for Seville and Valencia.

Spaniards observe a “day of reflection” on the eve of the vote. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power

Eoghan Gilmartin

Freelance journalist based in Madrid and host of the Sobremesa podcast

Vox has often been portrayed in international coverage as a party of Franco nostalgists whose ultraconservative Catholicism and civil-war rhetoric towards the separatist Catalan “enemy within” threatened a return to the worst of Spain’s recent past.

Yet since its disappointing showing at the 2023 general election, Abascal has purged much of the party’s original leadership and overseen an ideological renewal.

In looking to update its messaging, Vox has blended elements of Marine Le Pen’s welfare chauvinism, such as the concept of “national priority”, with ideas coming from the pan-European, white nationalist identitarian movement.

Virtually absent from Spanish political debate a year ago, national priority would give Spaniards preferential access to social housing, public services and welfare benefits, with Vox already securing PP backing for the principle in regional coalition deals.

In September, however, the European Commission warned that even the residence-based criteria used at a regional level could discriminate against citizens of other EU member states. Vox’s general election manifesto goes further, pledging to exclude all non-Spanish citizens from the country’s minimum-income benefit.

If the polls are right, PP’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo could become prime minister on a lower vote share than the PP secured in the last election. He would then owe his majority to Vox’s surge and support in coalition, and Abascal would have both the leverage and the incentive to show his voters what the party can deliver in office.

A coalition formed on those terms could also foreshadow a closer alliance between conservatives and the far right at a European level. A Le Pen victory in the French presidential election next spring would put the nationalist right at the head of one of the EU’s two most influential states, shifting the political centre of gravity in Brussels and opening the way for a durable governing bloc to the right of the EU’s traditional grand coalition.

It was not by chance that Vox opened its election campaign with a rally displaying video messages of support from Le Pen, Meloni and AfD’s Alice Weidel. Having drawn on its far-right European allies to reinvent itself, Vox could now in turn strengthen their hand if it is successful in becoming the PP’s kingmaker after Sunday’s vote.

Sánchez’s defeat would also deprive the centre left of its strongest counterweight in the European Council, where he is the only social democrat to represent one of the EU’s major powers.

Speaking to the Vox rally, Weidel proclaimed: “All of Europe is waiting for a political change in Madrid.” All of Europe may not be waiting for such a change, but it is certainly watching.

Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more

Ashifa Kassam

European community affairs correspondent

Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.

Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said.

“But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.

“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”

On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.

Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.

No new polls are allowed to be published in Spain in the five days before a Spanish election, but one company has found a surprising solución alternativa.

The Adelaide Review ran from 1984 to 2020, covering the city’s cultural and artistic life until Covid and upheavals in the media world made it “untenable”, its editor, Amanda Pepe, wrote in the final edition.

But now it has found unexpected new life as an, erm, back passage for Spanish polls in the blackout period.

The Review site is now owned by a company called Prensa Ibérica, which also runs the Spanish newspaper El Periódico.

An article on the Periódico website that links to the poll criticises “outdated legislation” that lets political parties see polls, but not citizens.

“The Adelaide Review’s daily poll addresses this issue, giving citizens access to the same information used by politicians,” it said.

Join us Sunday night for live blog on 2026 Spanish election

Jakub Krupa

It’s probably a good moment to say that we will be running a special Europe live blog from Madrid on Sunday night to bring you all the latest in the Spanish parliamentary election, including first polls, projections, reactions, and analysis.

Make sure to tune in on Sunday late afternoon and evening.

'I can’t conceive of us losing,' Sánchez says despite adverse polling

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported.

Amid a legal ban on publishing new opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.

“I can’t conceive of us losing,” Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.

However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.

Spain’s ‘rambling’ closing debate sparks row over opposition leader’s ‘sexist’ remark

Sam Jones

in Madrid

Last night’s debate between the leaders of Spain’s four biggest political parties was a rambling, ratty and revealing spectacle in which Ada Colau, the leader of the leftwing Broad Front, is generally agreed to have come out on top.

Colau, a former Barcelona mayor, was committed and forensic in her attacks on Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, over his refusal to condemn gender-based violence.

She and the socialist leader and current prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, also joined forces to question the economic wisdom of the far-right party’s plans for €112bn of public spending costs, and to defend the benefits of immigration.

Sánchez – who was far more animated and engaged in this debate than in last week’s head-to-head with Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP) – was happy to wind up his rival over his lack of English skills.

Before Feijóo could answer a question from Colau about the PP’s proposed tax cuts, Sánchez – a fluent English speaker – quipped:

“I’m sorry to say that Mr Feijóo’s maths are about as good as his English.”

Vox’s Abascal was keen to keep the focus on immigration and on corruption – a problem, he added, “that ruins and kills”.

He argued that his 30-year political career was unblemished by corruption allegations while suggesting that Sánchez was a “corruption magnet”. That led the prime minister to bring up the infamous mid-1990s holiday photos that show Feijóo hanging out on a boat with his friend Marcial Dorado, who was later convicted of drug trafficking.

But the biggest moment of the night came when Colau asked Feijóo how he could claim to be a good leader when his party had doggedly stood by Carlos Mazón, the PP president of the Valencia region who was eventually forced to resign over his disastrous handling of the floods two years ago that killed more than 230 people.

“Look, good management is taking charge in a national emergency and not running away from Paiporta,” Feijóo said in reference to Sánchez’s hasty exit from one of the areas that was worst hit by the floods after angry locals pelted him with mud during a visit shortly after the disaster.

But it was what came next that caused a stir. Turning to Colau – who, by the time of the floods in the autumn of 2024, had left the Barcelona mayoralty and no longer held public office – Feijóo said, “Y usted calladita” which translates as, “And there wasn’t a peep out of you”.

He accompanied those words putting his finger to his lips – a gesture some took to be a sexist shushing of the Broad Front leader.

Although Feijóo seemed to be trying to claim that Colau had remained silent over the floods when they happened, some took his words as an attempt to tell her to be quiet.

Sánchez was quick to pounce. “Why are you saying, ‘Not a peep out of you’, Mr Feijóo?” the prime minister asked the PP leader. “What kind of sexism is that, Mr Feijóo,” Sánchez added.

Feijóo accused Sánchez of trying to twist his words, but the damage was done. Speaking after the debate, the PP leader issued a semi-apology.

“If I’ve offended anyone, I of course take it back,” he said, adding that he hadn’t been telling Colau to be quiet. But he couldn’t resist arguing that Sánchez leftwing allies had kept quiet “during all the years of corruption”.

Colau herself said the PP leader’s words undermined his supposed feminist credentials. Speaking after the debate, she said:

“I think it was very clear what [Feijóo] was trying to do when he said ‘calladita’. That clearly sexist behaviour was witnessed on TV by all of Spain … As women we will not stop and we will not shut up. No one will make us shut up and we will go and vote.”

And since Spain’s Pedro Sánchez skipped the summit altogether as he’s dramatically fighting for his future ahead of this Sunday’s parliamentary election…

… let’s cross to Madrid for an update on last night’s TV debate…

EU budget talks break down, set to resume in mid-December

In yesterday’s blog, I promised to give you an update this morning on the EU summit, which continued into the small hours.

Well, not much happened, as the talks on the bloc’s next budget collapsed with no agreement, with a group of countries reportedly refusing to take part in further pointless meetings.

The format set the “Sensible Seven” of frugal countries against “Friends of Cohesion” calling for sustained EU spending. With a bit of theatre, everyone disagreed with everyone, and the talks broke down shortly after midnight.

Hungary’s PM Péter Magyar said the discussions would resume at the next summit in December, but warned “there seems to be little chance of reaching a compromise on the EU’s seven-year budget.”

But Germany’s Friedrich Merz tried to stay upbeat:

“Views on the EU budget still differ widely. What is needed now is realism and goodwill. I am confident that we can reach an agreement this year – for a strong economy and a secure Europe.”

There is a bit of urgency there, as France’s Emmanuel Macron wants the discussion on the bloc’s new €1.78tn budget for 2028-2034 to be agreed before the end of the year, and well clear of the French parliamentary elections next spring.

Nato jets scrambled after drone 'briefly' enters Latvian airspace from Russia

Overnight, Nato fighter jets and an interceptor drone were scrambled overnight in Latvia after a drone briefly entered the country’s airspace near its border with Russia, the army said.

Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, several countries bordering the conflict have reported incursions or drone and missile crashes on their territory.

This year, two drones were shot down over Latvia by Nato fighter jets, which protect the skies of Baltic states, Reuters reported.

An army statement said that during the night from Thursday to Friday a drone “briefly flew over Latvian territory” near the border with Russia.

“Fighter jets from Nato’s air-policing mission in the Baltic States were scrambled, and an interceptor drone from the national armed forces was deployed,” it said, without specifying the origin of the drone.

Morning opening: Putin 'cannot be a friend,' Zelenskyy says on Trump's comments

Jakub Krupa

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that US president Donald Trump comment’s hailing Russia’s Vladimir Putin as a friend is “the same that somebody’d say about Hitler during the second world war that he’s a good friend.”

Talking to BBC in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said Trump’s comments were “strange,” adding:

“He’s an aggressor … and a killer. He cannot be a friend. Just cannot be.”

In a pointed criticism of the US position, he said:

“We need American position to be American. We don’t need signals – I mean from the US – which we can get from Russia.”

Urging the US to use its “power and respect” to push Moscow more, he said:

“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right.”

His latest comments come as Russian attacks on Ukraine continue, amid growing concern over the upcoming winter as the strikes repeatedly hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

I will bring you more on this throughout the day.

I will also update you on last night’s EU summit, the final TV debate in Spain ahead of Sunday’s elections, and many more.

It’s Friday, 27 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.body:
Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.

The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.

The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.

The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February.

Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers.

In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”

He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”.

However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted.

In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks.

It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.”

The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet.

Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air, whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic.

Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners.

However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

articles.title: Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, succumbing to aviation fuel costs
articles.summary: The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.

articles.body:
Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy amid rising fuel costs

November 27, 2026

The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.

Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.

The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.

Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.

What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?

Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.

But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.

The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran.

Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?

Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.

In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.

It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.

This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

articles.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
articles.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could determine the political fortunes of a powerful dynasty. Victims' families hope to see justice.
articles.preview: November 27, 2026 Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could determine the political fortunes of a powerful dynasty. Victims' families hope to see justice. Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.
articles.body:
November 27, 2026

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could determine the political fortunes of a powerful dynasty. Victims' families hope to see justice.

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.

For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.

It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.

Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.

Why is Duterte on trial?

Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.

During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.

Human rights groups, however, found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction; [that] made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even through extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.

A 'way of governing through killing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defense. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country," Johnson said. "These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control."

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame in the US, told DW.

Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.

His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.

"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it," Arguelles said.

Why was Duterte arrested?

Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.

The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.

For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.

What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.

Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unraveled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.

Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.

In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.

What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.

Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.

Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University in the Philippines and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.

For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.

"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip," she said. "The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice."

articles.title: In Iran, child marriage risks complicated by war
articles.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.
